paper_title: The Aesthetic Implications of Complexity Theory in Regard to Object Creation and Haptic Response
venue: PhD Doctorate Thesis, Queensland College of Art, Griffith University
abstract: This research explores the idea of complexity for the express purpose of contributing to and expanding upon the lexicons of Art and Design. This exploration of complexity is undertaken by questioning a sensorial response to complex form, particularly through touch. The question in plain terms is, do we like to touch simple things or complex things? Touch is of course but one aspect of the suite of haptic senses, so proprioceptive, vestibular, and kinaesthetic senses are addressed, as is the deep and intertwined relationship between hapticity and sight. The research methodology is practice-led and has encompassed the methods of action research and participant study. I offer that the primary contributions to research are in the method of dialogue between creative practitioner and fractal algorithms expressed through novel technical methods of procedure explored and conveyed through object and through analysis in this thesis.
methodology: The research is practice-led, employing methods of action research and participant study. It involves generating mathematically derived (fractal) forms using software (Xenodream, Geomagic, Rhinoceros, Adobe After Effects, Vue xStream) and physical fabrication (3D printing in various materials like polyamide, ABS plastic, gypsum, bronze, and resin). The study design included an observational study and a short written questionnaire. Participants interacted with physical objects and surfaces, first unseen (tactile response) and then visually (visual response). The objects were designed to have varying degrees of complexity and were post-processed to achieve uniform surface texture (sanded and coated with acrylic lacquer for some, patinated for bronze). Fractal dimension (D value) was calculated using box counting methods (ImageJ for 2D images, Benoit for Matlab for 3D objects). The research also involved creating artist's books, holograms, and immersive video to explore different modes of aesthetic engagement.
sample: 25 participants were recruited for the main participant study, after an initial trial of 6 participants. Participants included university students, artists, lecturers, tutors, and a few persons with no connection to art, design, or the university. Demographics (age, gender, occupation/level of study) were collected (e.g., 19-year-old female, 25-year-old male, 38-year-old female, 24-year-old female, 60-year-old female, 21-year-old male, 28-year-old female, 35-year-old female, 44-year-old female).
manipulated_features: Fractal forms and surfaces with varying degrees of complexity (D values).
Low relief surfaces (4 types) with varying degrees of complexity, texture, and patterning.
Hand-held objects (4 types) of varying form and complexity, scaled to fit the average human hand (not longer than 90mm, not wider than 70mm).
Materials: Polyamide, ABS plastic, gypsum, bronze, resin, rag paper, metallic paper.
Surface treatments: sanded, acrylic lacquer, patinated, polished.
Visual renderings: point cloud plots, volumetric Perlin noise algorithms, texture maps, lighting parameters, monochrome vs. color.
Exhibition context: objects presented for touch vs. visual-only, artist's books, holograms, immersive video.
outcomes: Aesthetic preference for tactile interaction (surfaces and objects).
Aesthetic preference for visual interaction (surfaces and objects).
Qualitative feedback on reasons for preference.
Observation of participant response time and emotive signals (facial cues).
Correlation between tactile and visual preferences.
key_findings: Participants generally preferred to touch objects of lower fractal complexity (lower D value) and to see objects of higher fractal complexity.
For tactile preference, Object 1 (a holonic quaternion fractal with D value of 2.3) was preferred by 64% of participants (16 out of 25). Responses were quick, under 3 seconds.
For visual preference, Object 4 (the most complex object in the series) was preferred by 88% of participants (22 out of 25). Visual responses were generally slower and more considered.
A 'cognitive disconnect' was reported by some participants, where their tactile preference conflicted with their visual preference for the same object.
Objects that invited stroking and grasping, through moderate levels of structural and texture complexity, were viewed as most inviting to touch (referencing Klatzky and Peck's conclusion).

Bronze castings, due to their perceptible weight and material connotations, engaged tactile and kinaesthetic senses more effectively than lighter plastic prints. The bronze cast with patina and no polishing was least preferred visually, but the polished version received greater attention.

Shell-like forms were preferred over abstract quaternion forms due to their seeming association with real shells, enticing participants to look at and hold them. The delicacy of the shell wall contributed to visual and tactile appeal.

Monochrome point cloud renderings of highly complex fractal structures on rag paper were found to be aesthetically engaging, possibly due to perceived 'simplicity in complexity' and effective contrast extraction by the brain, allowing for cognitive engagement without immediate conceptual conclusion.
The immersive video 'The Walls' provided a haptic experience through vestibular senses, suggesting that non-linear systems can speak to the dynamism of life beyond traditional design conventions.
theories_referenced: Edge of Chaos theory (Michael Waldrop, Christopher Langton)
Aesthetics (George Birkhoff, Rudolf Arnheim, Immanuel Kant, Edmund Burke, Alva Noë)
Haptic Perception/Phenomenology (Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Jacques Derrida, Roberta Klatzky, Susan Lederman, Mark Paterson)
Cognitive Creativity (Ronald Finke, Thomas Ward, Steven Smith, Scott Barry Kaufman, Margaret Boden)
Hyperreality/Simulacra (Jean Baudrillard, Gilles Deleuze, Umberto Eco)
mechanisms: Sensorial engagement: Proprioceptive, vestibular, kinaesthetic, and tactile senses are addressed, along with their intertwined relationship with sight.
Dialogue between internal and external systems of complexity: Perceptual and cognitive systems are complex systems themselves, understanding patterns through internal patterned systems.

Resonant structures: Humans are drawn to intrinsic beauty in aspects of the world that offer bounded infinity, borders of change, and resonant structures, which operate by the same rules as human cognitive processes.

Efficient coding: Maximally efficient coding is observed for complex natural stimuli to which sensory systems are adapted during evolution, development, and adaptation, suggesting neurological wiring to perceive complexity.
Cognitive dissonance: Conflict between perceptual input (e.g., tactile) and cognitive models (e.g., visual associations) can lead to a 'logical dilemma'.

Associative memory: Memory is distributed and content-addressable, with neural cliques forming self-similar and recursively interconnected fractal structures that serve as associative pathways. Novel forms are processed by referencing existing memories.

Cross-sensory perception: Integration of information from visual and haptic pathways, with somatosensory evoked regions activated by objects whether touched or seen, suggesting a 'resonant cognition' of objects.

Play and exploration: Divergent creative processes and experimentation, not bounded by formalist logic, are crucial for generating new ideas and findings, leading to 'surprise' as a fundamental necessity for the creative act.
limitations: The participant study was qualitative in nature, with a limited sample size (25 participants), thus not aiming for accurate quantifiable outcomes regarding degrees of preference.
The analysis of fractal dimension for 3D forms lacked precise validity due to the complexities of translation and optimization processes from point cloud generation to 3D printing.

Losses of fidelity were expected and occurred during the translation of digital forms to physical prints, meaning the final objects might not perfectly retain their original mathematically generated dimensional values.
The study acknowledged the subjective role of the designer in the creation process, which may have influenced results despite attempts at impartiality.
Audience responses in exhibition settings can be influenced by politeness and context, making it difficult to elicit 'true' feedback.
The animations produced were not descriptive or documentary, which might have made them too abstract or puzzling for some viewers, leading to limited feedback.
The research acknowledges that communicating the ontology and epistemology of non-linear practice within a structured discourse is a challenge.
design_implications: Fractal principles (self-similarity, recursion, iteration) should be incorporated into compositional strategies for static and moving images, informing structure based on viewer psychology.
Design should consider the aesthetic preferences for fractal ranges, particularly the finding that people prefer to touch simple things but see complex things.
Objects designed for haptic interaction should aim for moderate levels of structural and texture complexity to invite stroking and grasping, and possess perceptible weight.
The use of generative design tools and algorithms can afford new possibilities for form creation, moving beyond traditional CAD constraints and fostering 'play' and 'discovery' in the design process.
Designers should be aware of the 'cognitive disconnect' between visual and tactile preferences for complex forms and consider how to bridge this gap through material choices and presentation.
The aesthetic appeal of 'simplicity in complexity' (e.g., sparse point cloud renderings with clear edges) can be leveraged in design to engage neural processes efficiently.

Artist's books and similar multimedia formats can serve as effective vehicles for exploring complex forms, engaging multiple senses (visual, haptic) and associative memory to create meaningful experiences.

The integration of complexity theory and fractal mathematics into art and design lexicon is crucial for advancing aesthetic theory and understanding human perceptual systems in relation to natural and algorithmically generated forms.
Immersive environments and interactive objects can provide novel haptic experiences, engaging vestibular senses and promoting a deeper understanding of complex forms.
